identity.title: First Millimeter Flares Detected from ϵ Eridani with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array

paper_type_evidence.quote: We report the detection of three large millimeter flaring events from the nearby Sun-like, $\epsilon$ Eridani, found in archival ALMA 12m and ACA observations at 1.33 mm

In this paper, we analyze archival observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) full 12-m array and Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of $\epsilon$ Eridani and report the discovery of three millimeter flaring events.

findings_qualitative.value: First detection of millimeter flares from a Sun-like (K2V) star, epsilon Eridani.

evidence.quote: This is the first time that flares have been detected from a Sun-like star at millimeter wavelengths.

findings_qualitative.value: The three detected flares have short, symmetric Gaussian temporal profiles (t_1/2 < 10 s) with little exponential decay, similar to M dwarf millimeter flares.

evidence.quote: The Gaussian fits reveal symmetric temporal structures and show that there is little exponential decay following the flare peak. This is similar to the structure of the millimeter flares reported from other M dwarfs.

findings_qualitative.value: Events E1 and E2 exhibit positive spectral indices, similar to millimeter solar flares and differing from M dwarf flares which show steeply negative spectral indices.

evidence.quote: This positive spectral index is more similar to millimeter solar flares, differing from M dwarf flares also detected at millimeter wavelengths that exhibit steeply negative spectral indices.

evidence.loc: Nature of the Detected Millimeter Flares
evidence.quote: In our new sample, only event E3 shows a similar negative spectral index. In contrast, events E1 and E2 exhibit positive $\alpha$ values.

findings_qualitative.value: Two flare events are consistent with no net linear polarization, while event E2 shows marginally significant linear polarization.

evidence.quote: We note that two flare events are consistent with no net linear polarization, and a third event (E2) is marginally significant.

findings_qualitative.value: Previous millimeter measurements of excess flux from epsilon Eridani likely included significant flaring emission, and the flare-excluded excess of 257 +/- 34 uJy is consistent with extrapolated inner dust ring SED predictions.

evidence.loc: Constraints on Dust Emission from an Inner Debris Disk
evidence.quote: Given that the previous millimeter measurements are much in excess of what we report here, those values likely include significant flaring emission. Extrapolating the SED fits for the inner dust ring from (cite: Su:2017) yields a predicted flux at 1.3 mm of $\sim0.2-0.3$ mJy, strikingly consistent with what we determine here.

claims.hypothesis: Sun-like stars such as epsilon Eridani exhibit detectable flaring emission at millimeter wavelengths.
claims.experiment: Fit point source models to each integration of archival ALMA 12-m and ACA Band 6 visibilities using CASA uvmodelfit, flagging >3 sigma events and verifying sideband agreement within 20%.
claims.result: Detected three flares in the ALMA 12-m data with peak flux densities of 28 +/- 7 mJy (E1), 14 +/- 3 mJy (E2), and 9 +/- 2 mJy (E3), and durations t_1/2 of 7.9, 9.0, and 6.6 sec.
claims.finding: First detection of millimeter flares from a Sun-like star, with peak brightness >50x quiescent stellar luminosity and >10x brighter than solar millimeter flares.

evidence.quote: We report the detection of three large millimeter flaring events from the nearby Sun-like, $\epsilon$ Eridani, found in archival ALMA 12m and ACA observations at 1.33 mm

evidence.loc: Creating Light Curves and Identifying Flares
evidence.quote: During this flare, the star brightened by a factor of $50\times$ over quiescent values, reaching a peak flux density of $28\pm7$ mJy and peak luminosity of $3.4\pm 0.9 \times 10^{14}$ erg s$^{-1}$ Hz$^{-1}$.

claims.hypothesis: Millimeter flares from the K2V star epsilon Eridani share spectral and temporal properties with solar and M dwarf millimeter flares.
claims.experiment: Fit Gaussian profiles to flare light curves and fit point source models to upper/lower sidebands and XX/YY polarizations at flare peaks.
claims.result: Flares have short durations (<10 sec) with symmetric profiles; E1 and E2 have positive spectral indices (1.81 +/- 1.94 and 7.29 +/- 2.89) while E3 is negative (-2.83 +/- 2.33); E2 has |Q/I| > -0.48 +/- 0.15.
claims.finding: Temporal structures are short and symmetric like M dwarf flares, but positive spectral indices in E1 and E2 are more similar to solar millimeter flares than M dwarf flares.

evidence.quote: This positive spectral index is more similar to millimeter solar flares, differing from M dwarf flares also detected at millimeter wavelengths that exhibit steeply negative spectral indices.

evidence.loc: Nature of the Detected Millimeter Flares
evidence.quote: All of the new events are short with $t_{1/2}$ values $<10$ sec, while previously detected millimeter flares have $t_{1/2}$ values of $2-35$ sec (cite: MacGregor:2018a; MacGregor:2020).

claims.hypothesis: Millimeter flaring emission contributes to the apparent millimeter excess attributed to an unresolved inner debris disk around epsilon Eridani.
claims.experiment: Fit a point source model with uvmodelfit to all ALMA visibilities excluding the flaring intervals E1, E2, and E3, and compare with expected photospheric flux and inner dust SED predictions.
claims.result: Quiescent flux density is 787 +/- 45 uJy, representing an excess of 257 +/- 34 uJy above the 0.53 mJy photosphere, lower than previous millimeter measurements (1.2 +/- 0.3 and 1.08 mJy) and matching the ~0.2-0.3 mJy predicted for the inner dust ring.
claims.finding: Previous millimeter excess measurements likely included flaring emission; the flare-excluded excess matches predictions for the inner dust belt, though chromospheric and dust contributions remain unresolved.

why_this_data.value: epsilon Eridani is the closest Sun-like star hosting a tentative planet and debris disks, and has archival ALMA 12-m and ACA Band 6 observations originally targeting the outer debris disk.

evidence.quote: Given that it is the closest Sun-like star to Earth that hosts a tentative planet along with both inner and outer debris disks, the $\epsilon$ Eridani system has been a frequent target for ALMA. Archival observations are available using Band 6 (center wavelength of 1.3 mm) from both the full 12-m array and ACA.

why_this_method.value: Primary beam correction increases apparent noise at the edge of the image where the star is located (~18'' from pointing center), making image-plane significance difficult to judge; fitting visibilities directly at fine integration times captures short (<30 s) flares.

evidence.quote: Because the primary beam correction is applied uniformly, it not only ‘upweights’ any real signals but also increases the apparent noise at the edges of the image (as can be seen in the right panel if Fig. 1) making it difficult to determine the uncertainty and judge significance levels. As a result, we choose to fit the visibilities directly to determine the stellar flux and search for any flare candidates

evidence.loc: Creating Light Curves and Identifying Flares
evidence.quote: However, millimeter flares have so far proven to be short events (typically lasting $<30$ sec), so fine time resolution is needed in order to fully characterize their temporal behavior.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Measuring stellar flux and searching for flares in the primary-beam-corrected image plane was rejected in favor of direct visibility fitting because primary beam correction increases apparent noise at the beam edge.

limitations_admitted.value: ACA has fewer and smaller (7-m) antennas, resulting in 3-5x higher rms noise per integration than the 12-m array, preventing detection of flares of this brightness in the ACA data.

evidence.quote: with fewer antennas in the array and smaller antenna diameters (7-m for the ACA), the total collecting area is reduced and as a result the rms noise in each integration was a factor of $3-5\times$ higher than for the ALMA 12-m observations.

limitations_admitted.value: Due to limited signal-to-noise, spectral index and fractional linear polarization lower limits can only be computed at the peak of the three flares, and lack of polarization calibration leads to large uncertainties.

evidence.quote: Due to limited signal-to-noise, we are only able to compute the spectral index and lower limit on the fractional linear polarization at the peak of the three detected flares.

limitations_admitted.value: The 12-m ALMA beam (~1.6'' or ~5 AU) cannot spatially resolve the proposed inner dust belts from the central star, so quiescent flux contains both chromospheric and dust contributions.

evidence.loc: Constraints on Dust Emission from an Inner Debris Disk
evidence.quote: The beam size in the 12-m ALMA observations is $\sim1.6\ensuremath{''}$ or $\sim5$ AU. The potential inner dust belt(s) have been proposed to extend from either 3–21 AU (cite: Greaves:2014) or 1.5–2 AU and 8–20 AU (cite: Backman:2009). In either of these two models, the inner dust would not be resolved from the central star by the existing ALMA observations.

referee_caveats_inferred: In the 12-m observations, the star is ~18 arcsec from the pointing center (at the edge of the primary beam), where primary beam attenuation, pointing errors, and off-axis instrumental polarization leakage are significant.

uvmodelfit does not automatically apply primary beam attenuation correction when fitting visibilities off-axis unless accounted for, and the paper does not state how primary beam response at 18 arcsec off-axis was applied to the uvmodelfit visibility fluxes.

Point source fitting with uvmodelfit on single 6-second integrations in a field containing extended debris disk emission could be affected by unmodeled disk structure if short baselines are not excluded or disk emission is not subtracted.

There is a date discrepancy in the text for the ACA observations: the Abstract says '2016 October 24-November 23' while Section 2.1 says '2015 October 24 and 2015 November 23' for project 2016.1.00803.S.

reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~20-50 GB (calibrated measurement sets for 4.4 hr of 12-m and 5 hr of ACA Band 6 continuum/TDM observations)
reproducibility.score_reason: Archival ALMA project codes are clearly stated and the core method (CASA uvmodelfit per integration on upper/lower sidebands and XX/YY polarizations) is conceptually simple, but the custom pipeline scripts, exact stellar position fixing in uvmodelfit, off-axis primary beam correction in visibility space, and exact time windows for E2/E3 are not specified.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: Both ALMA datasets (2013.1.00645.S and 2016.1.00803.S) are public in the archive, the core analysis relies on standard CASA tasks (tclean, uvmodelfit), and the main results are concrete numeric values (flare peak fluxes, durations, spectral indices, polarization limits, and quiescent stellar flux).
